doc.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, September 23, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: The clarinet and finding a voice
title: Having your own voice and who owns music
summary: Davern says a recognizable sound is essential; he tells the Bobby Hackett story about stealing from Armstrong and says music belongs to everybody.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: But you have a very distinct voice on that instrument. You’ve taken that instrument past any generic conception into this elusive category that all musicians seek called “voice.” And you have that.

Thank you. That I think is a prerequisite for anybody doing anything, is to put their “John Hancock” you know, once you’ve seen that signature it’s forever imprinted on your mind. And I think the only way you can ever establish yourself is to have something like the cookie cutter, according to that syndrome, is you must take it upon yourself to bite the bullet and say, for better or for worse, this is the way I sound. This is the sound that I make. And you must stand by it. And that’s why this, you know “you’re stealing my music,” or “this is MY—” If you can make your own noise on the instrument and make your own sound which is instantly recognizable within let’s say four bars, then you know, that’s it. Then you ain’t steal anybody’s anything. You might be a composite or a storehouse or a bank, you know, a depository of all you’ve heard and all that’s come before and all you’ve chosen to absorb. But once music is out there, you can do this. And I think that’s the most important thing is to get what you’ve listened to, what impressed you most, what moved you most, and make it into your own thing. When Louis Armstrong died, Walter Cronkite when he was anchor on CBS had Dizzy Gillespie and Miles Davis and I think Buck Clayton and Bobby Hackett to name a few, this was in 1971, and he asked them well, “How did Louis Armstrong influence you?” So everybody, like Miles Davis says you know, “We’d all be digging ditches if it wasn’t for Louis.” And when he got to Bobby Hackett he said how did he influence you, and he says, “Well,” he says, with that New England accent he says, “Well I spent half my life,” he says, “stealing everything I could from him, and the other half covering it up.” But that’s it. I mean nobody, no one person can claim anything. Once it’s out there, it becomes everybody’s.
Correct, it becomes music, and music is for everybody, for all.
